title: Pleuritic chest pain during a daytime fast

source.citation: Mendelsohn RA, Taveras AN, Mazer BA, Clayton LM. Euglycemic Diabetic Ketoacidosis Precipitated by SGLT-2 Inhibitor Use, Pericarditis, and Fasting: A Case Report. Clin Pract Cases Emerg Med. 2020;4(3):389-392.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Three days of substernal chest pain
presentation.hpi: Three days of constant substernal chest pain that is worse on inspiration and when leaning forward, with palpitations; the pain does not radiate. For the past 10 days he has kept a strict daytime fast for Ramadan. No infectious or neurological symptoms, shortness of breath, abdominal pain or dysuria.
pmh: Type 2 diabetes mellitus, not on insulin
No connective tissue disorder; no recent surgery
presentation.social: Denies alcohol, tobacco and illicit drug use. Only recent travel was a four-hour flight two weeks ago.
presentation.family: Father with type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease and early coronary artery disease.

exam: Tachycardic; normal first and second heart sounds without murmurs, rubs or gallops
Normal capillary refill; no peripheral edema
Receiving 2 L/min oxygen by nasal cannula at the time of the first vital signs (SpO2 100%)

imaging.finding: Tiny pericardial effusion with inflammatory changes suspicious for pericarditis; no pulmonary embolism

ecg: Sinus tachycardia; marked ST elevation in the precordial leads, minimal ST elevation in the limb leads, ST depression in aVR and widespread PR-segment depression; no ectopy, axis and intervals otherwise normal

diagnosis.primary: Euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis due to empagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor), precipitated by daytime fasting and acute coxsackievirus pericarditis

management: IV ketorolac (Toradol) for the pericarditic pain, with relief
Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate sent because of the SGLT2 inhibitor; empagliflozin stopped immediately
ICU admission on an IV insulin infusion with dextrose-containing maintenance fluid
Later in the admission: large pericardial effusion drained by emergency pericardiocentesis with a pigtail catheter
outcome: Acidosis improved and the anion gap closed over two days; serum PCR was positive for coxsackievirus A and B. Discharged home on hospital day 5, with empagliflozin replaced by glipizide alongside metformin.
teachingPoints: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause diabetic ketoacidosis with a normal or only mildly raised glucose; check the anion gap and blood ketones in any unwell patient taking one.
Typical precipitants are reduced intake (fasting, ketogenic diets), acute illness, surgery, insulin dose reduction and alcohol; several often combine.
Measure blood beta-hydroxybutyrate: the urine nitroprusside dipstick detects acetoacetate only and can underestimate ketosis.
Treat as DKA (fluids, insulin infusion, potassium) but give dextrose with the insulin from the start; stop the SGLT2 inhibitor.
Do not anchor on an obvious diagnosis: an unexplained high anion gap acidosis needs its own explanation.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of his metabolic acidosis?
questions.extra: ECG: diffuse ST elevation with PR depression. Serum HCO3⁻ 12 mmol/L, anion gap 22, glucose 158 mg/dL, lactate 1.3 mmol/L. ABG: pH 7.22, PaCO2 20.5 mm Hg.
options: Starvation ketosis from the daytime fast
Lactic acidosis from low cardiac output
questions.explanation: A normal lactate rules out lactic acidosis, whether from metformin or poor perfusion, and fasting alone causes only mild ketosis (bicarbonate rarely below 18 mmol/L). An SGLT2 inhibitor plus reduced intake plus an acute illness is the classic setting for euglycemic DKA; the 2024 ADA/EASD/JBDS/AACE/DTS consensus report on hyperglycemic crises accepts known diabetes in place of hyperglycemia for the diagnosis.

questions.q: Which test best confirms the suspected diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Beta-hydroxybutyrate is the dominant ketone in DKA; the nitroprusside dipstick detects acetoacetate and acetone only, so it can underestimate ketosis. The 2024 consensus report prefers blood beta-hydroxybutyrate (3.0 mmol/L or more supports DKA); here it was 116 mg/dL, about 11 mmol/L.

questions.q: Which treatment plan is most appropriate?
questions.extra: Serum beta-hydroxybutyrate 116.1 mg/dL (reference 0.21–2.8 mg/dL); glucose 158 mg/dL.
options: IV fluids only; start insulin once glucose exceeds 250 mg/dL
IV sodium bicarbonate to raise the pH above 7.30 first
Subcutaneous basal insulin and encourage oral intake
Stop empagliflozin; IV fluids with insulin and dextrose infusions
questions.explanation: Ketoacidosis resolves only with insulin; because glucose is already near normal, dextrose must run with the insulin infusion from the start, and the SGLT2 inhibitor is stopped (2024 consensus report; JBDS DKA guidance). Bicarbonate is not recommended at pH 7.22, and waiting for hyperglycemia leaves ketogenesis untreated.

questions.q: How should his blood gas be interpreted?
questions.extra: ABG: pH 7.22, PaCO2 20.5 mm Hg, HCO3⁻ 8.3 mmol/L.
options: Metabolic acidosis with appropriate respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis with a concurrent respiratory acidosis
Metabolic acidosis with a concurrent respiratory alkalosis
Primary respiratory alkalosis with metabolic compensation
questions.explanation: Winter's formula predicts PaCO2 = 1.5 × HCO3⁻ + 8 ± 2 = 18.5–22.5 mm Hg; the measured 20.5 mm Hg fits, so there is no second respiratory disorder. The acidemic pH excludes a primary respiratory alkalosis.

evidence.quote: A 39-year-old male … presented to our ED complaining of three days of substernal chest pain
a history of hyperlipidemia and non-insulin-dependent type 2 diabetes mellitus managed with metformin and empagliflozin
He reported that the pain was constant, worsening on inspiration and while leaning forward, and associated with palpitations.
for the preceding 10 days he had been maintaining a strict daytime fast for the religious holiday of Ramadan
He denied radiation of his pain, infectious symptoms, neurological symptoms, shortness of breath, abdominal pain, or dysuria.
He also denied any history of connective tissue disorder. He had no recent surgical history.
His family history was significant for a father with type 2 diabetes, chronic kidney disease, and early coronary artery disease.
The patient denied use of alcohol, tobacco, or illicit drugs of any kind. His only recent travel was a four-hour flight two weeks prior.
afebrile, tachycardic, and hypertensive (97.8^o Fahrenheit, 116 beats per minute, 148/96 millimeters of mercury
15 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation of 100% on 2 liters nasal cannula
His cardiac examination revealed tachycardia with normal first and second heart sounds, no murmurs, rubs, or gallops.
He had normal capillary refill in his extremities and no peripheral edema.
The rest of his physical examination was otherwise benign.

Initial electrocardiogram revealed sinus tachycardia, significant ST-segment elevation in the precordial leads, minimal ST-segment elevation in the limb leads, ST depression in aVR, and widespread PR-segment depression.
There was no evidence of ectopy, and the axis and intervals were otherwise normal.
leukocytosis of 13.1 × 10⁹ per liter (/L) (5.0–10.0 × 10⁹/L), negative troponin
C-reactive protein of 30.43 milligrams per deciliter (mg/dL) (0–0.74 mg/dL) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 75 millimeters per hour (mm/h)
CTA of the chest revealed tiny pericardial effusion with some inflammatory changes suspicious for pericarditis and no evidence of pulmonary emboli.
he was given a dose of intravenous toradol with subsequent improvement in his chest pain
Critically, he also had a high anion-gap acidosis with bicarbonate of 12 millimoles per liter (mmol/L) (22–32 mmol/L), anion gap of 22
serum glucose of 158 mg/dL (74–118 mg/dL) and an arterial blood gas showing a pH of 7.22 (7.35–7.45), partial pressure of carbon dioxide 20.5 mmHg

evidence.field: investigations[PaO2 (on 2 L/min oxygen)], investigations[Bicarbonate (arterial blood gas)], investigations[Lactate]
evidence.quote: partial pressure of oxygen 115.3 mmHg (75–100 mmHg), and bicarbonate of 8.3 mmol/L (22–27 mmol/L). His lactate was normal at 1.3 mmol/L
Cognizant of recent reports of eDKA associated with SGLT-2 inhibitors such as empagliflozin, we sent a serum beta-hydroxybutyrate level
which returned at 116.1 mg/dl (0.21–2.8 mg/dL), confirming our suspicion for eDKA
His empagliflozin was stopped immediately, and he was admitted to the intensive care unit on intravenous (IV) drips of insulin and dextrose-containing maintenance fluid.
This patient presented with eDKA in the setting of SGLT-2 inhibitor use, daytime fasting, and acute pericarditis.
While being treated for eDKA, the patient's pericarditis was treated with oral colchicine.
Over the next two days, his acidosis improved and his anion gap closed.
he developed a large pericardial effusion, which required emergency pericardiocentesis with placement of a pigtail pericardial drain
Serum polymerase chain reaction was positive for multiple strains of coxsackievirus A and B.
The patient was discharged home on hospital day five with his medication changed to metformin and glipizide.
